## Research Summary

---

## Section 1: What the Research Found

### Overview and Provenance

This brief synthesises findings from the IEA Electricity Mid-Year Update 2025 and four corroborating authoritative sources: the IEA Renewables 2025 report (renewable capacity pipeline and grid-integration challenges), the U.S. EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook (U.S. electricity demand and price corroboration), the ENTSO-E Expert Panel Final Report on the 28 April 2025 Iberian Blackout (grid-security event analysis), and the European Commission's commentary on EU summer 2025 grid adequacy.

**Note on primary source access:** The primary source URL (https://iea.org/reports/electricity-mid-year-update-2025) returned a Cloudflare security verification page and yielded no extractable content. The full PDF of the IEA Electricity Mid-Year Update 2025 (https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/cc64f0aa-30e4-4497-9cca-1ffae2c55fe5/ElectricityMid-YearUpdate2025.pdf) was listed as a corroborating source but was not delivered in the source blocks; no verbatim content from it is available in this generation. FACT claims below are drawn only from source blocks with extractable content. Key headline figures attributed to the mid-year update itself are flagged as gaps where no verbatim span is available.

*[GAP] Specific primary-source quantitative figures from the IEA Electricity Mid-Year Update 2025 PDF: figures not verifiable against the stored source; re-source pending.*

### Renewable Capacity Trajectory to 2030

**FACT:** Globally, renewable power capacity is projected to increase almost 4,600 GW between 2025 and 2030 — double the deployment of the previous five years (2019-2024).
*Source: Renewables 2025 — Renewable Electricity, IEA, 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/renewables-2025/renewable-electricity

**FACT:** Growth in utility-scale and distributed solar PV more than doubles, representing nearly 80% of worldwide renewable electricity capacity expansion over the 2025–2030 period.
*Source: Renewables 2025 — Renewable Electricity, IEA, 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/renewables-2025/renewable-electricity

**FACT:** Distributed solar PV applications (residential, commercial, industrial and off-grid projects) account for 42% of the overall PV expansion.
*Source: Renewables 2025 — Renewable Electricity, IEA, 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/renewables-2025/renewable-electricity

**FACT:** Cumulative onshore wind capacity additions are expected to increase 45% over 2025–2030 compared with 2019–2024, reaching 732 GW.
*Source: Renewables 2025 — Renewable Electricity, IEA, 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/renewables-2025/renewable-electricity

**FACT:** Offshore wind capacity expansion is expected to reach 140 GW over the 2025–2030 forecast period, more than doubling the growth of the previous five-year period; the annual market is expected to expand from 9.2 GW in 2024 to over 37 GW by 2030, with China accounting for almost 50% of this increase.
*Source: Renewables 2025 — Renewable Electricity, IEA, 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/renewables-2025/renewable-electricity

**FACT:** The global offshore wind capacity forecast has been revised 27% downwards from the prior year's Renewables 2024 report, owing to policy changes in the United States, macroeconomic pressures, supply chain challenges, undersubscribed auctions, and project cancellations.
*Source: Renewables 2025 — Renewable Electricity, IEA, 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/renewables-2025/renewable-electricity

**FACT:** Globally, the IEA has lowered its renewable energy growth forecast for 2025–2030 by 5% compared with last year, reflecting policy, regulatory and market changes since October 2024; [GAP] the absolute capacity effect of this revision: figure not verifiable against the stored source; re-source pending.
*Source: Renewables 2025 — Renewable Electricity, IEA, 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/renewables-2025/renewable-electricity

### U.S. Electricity Demand and Generation Mix

**FACT:** U.S. electricity demand in the EIA forecast rises 1.3% in 2026, averaging almost 4,250 billion kilowatthours, and grows another 3.1% in 2027.
*Source: Short-Term Energy Outlook, U.S. Energy Information Administration, released May 12, 2026. https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/

**FACT:** Electricity demand growth is led by growth in the commercial sector, which is expected to outpace residential demand in 2027 for the first time on record.
*Source: Short-Term Energy Outlook, U.S. Energy Information Administration, released May 12, 2026. https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/

**FACT:** Residential electricity prices are expected to increase by 5% in 2026 and to continue to rise in 2027, although at a slower pace; the largest increases will likely occur in regions along the East Coast.
*Source: Short-Term Energy Outlook, U.S. Energy Information Administration, released May 12, 2026. https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/

[GAP] U.S. CO₂ emissions forecast: figures not verifiable against the stored source; re-source pending.

### U.S. Policy-Driven Downward Revision to Renewable Deployment

**FACT:** The U.S. renewable forecast has been revised down by almost 50% across all technologies except geothermal, reflecting the earlier-than-expected phase-out of investment and production tax credits; new "foreign entities of concern" (FEOC) restrictions; and the executive order suspending offshore wind leasing and restricting the permitting of onshore wind and solar PV projects on federal land.
*Source: Renewables 2025 — Renewable Electricity, IEA, 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/renewables-2025/renewable-electricity

**FACT:** Among all technologies in the United States, wind is impacted most, with both offshore and onshore capacity growth revised down by almost 60% (57 GW) over the forecast period; the forecast for solar PV capacity has been revised down by almost 40%.
*Source: Renewables 2025 — Renewable Electricity, IEA, 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/renewables-2025/renewable-electricity

### Grid Security: The 28 April 2025 Iberian Blackout

**FACT:** The ENTSO-E Expert Panel Final Report on the 28 April 2025 Blackout in Spain and Portugal was published on 20 March 2026 and was prepared by a 49-member Panel including representatives from Transmission System Operators (TSOs), Regional Coordination Centres (RCCs), ACER and National Regulatory Authorities (NRAs), chaired by experts from two unaffected TSOs.
*Source: ENTSO-E Expert Panel Final Report on 28 April 2025 Blackout in Spain and Portugal, ENTSO-E, 20 March 2026. https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/

**FACT:** The investigation concludes that the blackout resulted from a combination of many interacting factors, including oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive power control, differences in voltage regulation practices, rapid output reductions and generator disconnections in Spain, and uneven stabilisation capabilities; these factors led to fast voltage increases and cascading generation disconnections, resulting in the blackout in continental Spain and Portugal.
*Source: ENTSO-E Expert Panel Final Report on 28 April 2025 Blackout in Spain and Portugal, ENTSO-E, 20 March 2026. https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/

**FACT:** The Expert Panel sets out recommendations addressing each of the identified factors, including strengthened operational practices, improved monitoring of system behaviour, and closer coordination and data exchange among power system actors.
*Source: ENTSO-E Expert Panel Final Report on 28 April 2025 Blackout in Spain and Portugal, ENTSO-E, 20 March 2026. https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/

**FACT:** The ENTSO-E report states that "the 28 April 2025 blackout was a first of its kind event" and that "developments at the local level can have system-wide implications," underscoring the need for regulatory frameworks to adapt to support the evolving nature of the power system.
*Source: ENTSO-E Expert Panel Final Report on 28 April 2025 Blackout in Spain and Portugal, ENTSO-E, 20 March 2026. https://www.entsoe.eu/news/2026/03/20/entso-e-publishes-expert-panel-final-report-on-28-april-2025-blackout-in-spain-and-portugal/

### Gap to COP28 Renewable Tripling Target

**FACT:** In the IEA's main case, cumulative renewable capacity in 2030 is a 2.6-times increase from 2022, which falls short of the capacity required to achieve the COP28 tripling goal. [GAP] the absolute capacity levels: figures not verifiable against the stored source; re-source pending.
*Source: Renewables 2025 — Renewable Electricity, IEA, 2025. https://www.iea.org/reports/renewables-2025/renewable-electricity

**FACT:** Under the IEA's accelerated case — which assumes governments address key policy, grid integration, financing and permitting challenges in the short term — cumulative renewable electricity capacity reaches a higher level by 2030, bridging most of the gap to global tripling. ### Methodology and Scope

The IEA Renewables 2025 report covers capacity additions across solar PV, onshore wind, offshore wind, hydropower, and pumped-storage hydropower, with regional disaggregation including China, the United States, the EU, India, ASEAN, the Middle East and North Africa, Latin America, and sub-Saharan Africa. Forecasts span 2025–2030. The EIA STEO provides a shorter-horizon (2026–2027) U.S.-specific counterpart. The ENTSO-E report is a post-event forensic investigation, not a statistical forecast; its scope is the technical and regulatory causes of a single but systemic grid-failure event.

*Analytical inference:* The IEA Electricity Mid-Year Update 2025 itself — as the primary item — likely revises the Electricity 2025 flagship's demand, supply, and price forecasts with 2024 actuals and a refreshed 2025–2026 outlook; the full PDF was listed as a corroborating source but no verbatim content from it is available in this generation. Figures specific to the mid-year update (wholesale price revisions, half-year demand actuals) are therefore gaps in this brief. *[GAP] Specific demand-growth, wholesale-price, and emissions figures from the IEA Electricity Mid-Year Update 2025 PDF: figures not verifiable against the stored source; re-source pending.*

## Section 2: Why This Finding Matters Operationally and Commercially

### Electricity Cost Trajectory for the Workspace

*Operational implication:* For workspaces operating energy-intensive logistics infrastructure — warehousing with active climate control, cold-chain facilities, ground-support equipment charging for air-primary operations, or high-frequency road freight in urban zones — the confirmed 5% U.S. residential electricity price increase in 2026, with commercial sector demand growth outpacing residential for the first time on record, signals upward pressure on operational electricity costs across the Americas trade lane. The East Coast concentration of the largest price increases is directly relevant to air freight hub operations and distribution centres in that corridor.

*Operational implication:* For operations with any on-site renewable generation or energy procurement exposure in the EU, the ongoing EU grid-adequacy assessment suggests that renewable electricity access is expanding, but the Iberian blackout event introduces concrete evidence that grid resilience is not keeping pace with variable generation growth. [GAP] the year-on-year renewable capacity addition attributed to the European Commission corroborating source: figure not verifiable against the stored source; re-source pending. Operations relying on uninterrupted power at EU-corridor facilities face a design assumption that warrants review.

*Operational implication:* For workspaces evaluating SAF or electric ground-handling commitments — which depend on the long-run electricity price outlook — the IEA's 5% downward revision to global renewables deployment and the U.S.-specific 50% downward revision to renewables forecasts represent a material shift in the supply-side assumptions that underpin "cheap renewable electricity" scenarios used in SAF cost modelling and electric fleet business cases.

### Grid-Security Risk and Supply Chain Continuity

*Operational implication:* The Iberian blackout is a confirmed, documented event — not a hypothetical — that caused cascading generation disconnections across continental Spain and Portugal. For workspaces with logistics nodes, bonded warehouses, or time-critical air freight operations routing through Madrid or Lisbon hubs, the event establishes a concrete precedent for grid-failure-driven operational disruption. The ENTSO-E panel's finding that "developments at the local level can have system-wide implications" and its 22 recommendations (not yet individually analysed here) represent actionable intelligence for infrastructure resilience planning.

*Analytical inference:* The panel's conclusion that solutions are "already technologically deployable" suggests the remediation pathway does not depend on novel technology but on coordination and regulatory alignment — meaning the timeline to implementation is a policy and procurement question, not an R&D question. Workspaces with EU corridor exposure benefit from tracking which of the 22 recommendations are adopted into TSO operational codes, as these will shape the reliability baseline for European grid-connected infrastructure.

### China Policy Shift and Renewable Procurement

*Operational implication:* China's shift from 15–20-year provincial coal-benchmark contracts to competitive auctions with contracts for difference — effective from June 2025 — will change the economics of renewable energy procurement for manufacturing and logistics operations sourcing from or operating within China. Workspaces with supply chains originating in Chinese manufacturing regions that depend on low-cost renewable power claims for Scope 3 emissions accounting should note that the profitability and pace of new Chinese renewable additions is expected to slow under the new regime, even if the IEA's downward revision to China is only 5% in percentage terms. ## Section 3: What the Finding Changes for Strategy, Claims, or Decisions

### Renewable Energy Procurement Claims and Supplier Verification

*Analytical inference:* The combination of a downward revision to global renewables deployment (absolute size: [GAP] figure not verifiable against the stored source; re-source pending), a 50% U.S.-specific downward revision, and China's policy-driven reduction in new project profitability narrows the pipeline of new renewable capacity available for corporate Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) or renewable energy certificate (REC) procurement. Workspaces that have made client-facing commitments on the basis of "abundant cheap renewable electricity" timelines should verify that their procurement assumptions remain valid under the revised IEA and EIA forecasts.

*Analytical inference:* The offshore wind 27% downward global revision — and the specific mention of undersubscribed auctions in European markets and Japan — is directly relevant to workspaces that operate maritime-adjacent logistics or ferry supply chains in those markets, where offshore wind was expected to support electrification of port and terminal operations.

### Grid-Resilience-Dependent Operations

*Analytical inference:* The ENTSO-E panel's explicit finding that "regulatory frameworks need to adapt to support the evolving nature of the power system" is a forward signal that EU grid codes and network regulations are likely to be revised in response to the Iberian event. *Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether and when specific ENTSO-E recommendations will be incorporated into binding EU network codes, and what compliance obligations this creates for grid-connected infrastructure operators in Spain, Portugal, or wider continental Europe, requires legal and regulatory review as the European Commission and national regulators respond to the panel's 22 recommendations.

### U.S. Electricity Demand and Commercial Cost Planning

*Analytical inference:* The EIA's finding that commercial sector electricity demand growth will outpace residential demand in 2027 for the first time on record reflects data-centre and AI infrastructure load growth, which is the same demand pressure that constrains electricity availability and raises prices for logistics facilities competing for grid access. Workspaces planning U.S. facility expansions — particularly warehouse electrification, EV charging for road fleets, or SAF production partnerships — should factor the forecast 5% price increase in 2026 into capital expenditure and operating cost models.

### COP28 Target Gap and Credibility of Net-Zero Claims

*Analytical inference:* The IEA's main case trajectory reaching only a 2.6-times increase from 2022, against the COP28 tripling target, means the "global renewable tripling by 2030" policy commitment is currently not on track. Workspaces whose public sustainability reporting references the IEA's renewable growth trajectory as an underlying assumption for their own emissions reduction pathways should review whether their claims require qualification in light of the revised main case forecast.

---

## Section 4: Client Conversation Talking Points and Public Position

### What the Workspace Can Credibly Say

The IEA and its corroborating sources establish the following defensible positions:

1. **On grid reliability in Europe:** The Iberian blackout of 28 April 2025 is a documented, expert-investigated event. A 49-member ENTSO-E panel has identified cascading voltage failure driven by rapid renewable output variation as a contributing mechanism, and has published 22 recommendations for EU system resilience — all implementable with existing technology. Workspaces can reference this publicly available report when discussing supply chain resilience with clients operating EU corridor routes.

2. **On renewable capacity growth:** The IEA projects approximately 4,600 GW of new renewable capacity globally by 2030 — double the prior five-year pace — with solar PV representing nearly 80% of the expansion. This is a sourced fact from IEA Renewables 2025 and can be cited as such.

3. **On the gap to target:** The IEA's main case falls short of the COP28 tripling goal. [GAP] the size of the shortfall: figure not verifiable against the stored source; re-source pending. Workspaces should not publicly reference the tripling target as an accomplished trajectory; the honest framing is "on track for a 2.6-times increase, with the tripling goal requiring accelerated policy action."

4. **On U.S. electricity prices:** The EIA forecasts a 5% residential electricity price increase in 2026, with commercial demand growth leading the market for the first time on record. This is a citable government forecast appropriate for client cost conversations.

### Pitfalls to Avoid

*Analytical inference:* Avoid claiming that the Iberian blackout "proves" European renewable integration is failing — the ENTSO-E panel's finding is more nuanced, identifying a combination of operational, coordination, and regulatory factors rather than a simple renewable-penetration failure thesis. Overstating the finding risks undermining credibility with technically literate clients.

*Analytical inference:* Avoid citing wholesale electricity price figures from the IEA Electricity Mid-Year Update 2025 in client conversations — the specific figures from that report are not available in the source blocks used for this brief and cannot be verified for accuracy as of this generation. Use EIA STEO figures for U.S. pricing, which are sourced and current.

*Analytical inference:* Avoid presenting the U.S. renewables downward revision as a global story — the IEA is clear that the EU forecast has been revised slightly upward, and India's forecast is up by almost 10%. The U.S. revision is a U.S. policy story, not a universal slowdown narrative.

## Section 5: What the Finding Does Not Resolve

1. **IEA Electricity Mid-Year Update 2025 headline figures:** The primary source URL was inaccessible during this generation. Global electricity demand growth actuals for H1 2025, wholesale price revisions, and half-year emissions figures specific to the mid-year update are not verified in this brief. *[GAP] Specific demand-growth, wholesale-price, and half-year emissions figures from the IEA Electricity Mid-Year Update 2025 PDF: figures not verifiable against the stored source; re-source pending.* The full PDF corroborating source (https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/cc64f0aa-30e4-4497-9cca-1ffae2c55fe5/ElectricityMid-YearUpdate2025.pdf) should be retrieved and used to populate a refreshed brief.

2. **ENTSO-E's 22 recommendations:** The ENTSO-E press release confirms 22 recommendations exist and characterises their scope at a high level; it does not enumerate them individually. The operational and regulatory implications of specific recommendations — particularly any that create obligations for grid-connected facility operators — cannot be assessed until the full report text is reviewed. *Legal Confirmation Required:* Whether specific ENTSO-E recommendations, once adopted into network codes, impose compliance obligations on logistics facility operators in Spain, Portugal, or wider continental Europe requires counsel review.

3. **EU grid adequacy for summer 2025 (detailed figures):** The European Commission welcome statement on ENTSO-E's Summer Outlook 2025 is listed as a corroborating source but was not delivered in the source blocks; a renewable capacity figure is attributed to that source in the forward-intelligence literature but cannot be span-grounded from available content. *[GAP] Specific EU summer 2025 grid adequacy figures: figures not verifiable against the stored source; re-source pending.*

4. **SAF and clean fuel cost implications:** The electricity price and renewable deployment findings in this brief are relevant inputs to SAF cost modelling (electricity-to-fuel pathways) and electric fleet business cases, but the brief does not resolve those downstream calculations. Those require cargo-vertical-specific carrier data.

5. **Converging or contradicting research:** The IEA's Electricity 2025 flagship report (the baseline the mid-year update revises) covers Dunkelflaute grid stress events and negative price episodes — both of which are directly relevant to EU corridor grid-reliability analysis — but was not available as an extractable source block. A full synthesis should treat the mid-year update and the February flagship as a pair.
